← Commercial Photography Licensing Quote Calculator

How much more does a national or worldwide license cost than local?

Territory is one of the calculator's four usage-rights multipliers: 1× for local, 1.25× for national, 1.6× for worldwide. Nothing else about the shoot changes between the three rows below — only how widely the client can use the images.

Territory pricing on the same shoot

$1,200 creative fee, 6-month term, website/email/social only, non-exclusive, 5 final images, no rush. Territory is the only input changed row to row.
TerritoryMultiplierUsage rightsTotal quotePer-image allocation
Local / one city1×$420.00$1,620.00$84.00
Country / national1.25×$525.00$1,725.00$105.00
Worldwide1.6×$672.00$1,872.00$134.40

Usage rights = creative fee × 35% × channel factor × term factor × territory multiplier × exclusivity multiplier × (1 + rush% ÷ 100). Only the territory multiplier changes across this table; channel factor, term factor, and exclusivity multiplier are all held at 1× and rush at 0%.

National territory adds exactly 25% to the usage-rights line over local, because the multiplier moves from 1× to 1.25× and every other factor is unchanged — $525.00 is $420.00 plus a quarter of $420.00. Worldwide adds 60%, the same relationship at 1.6×: $672.00 is $420.00 plus 60% of $420.00. The creative/production fee itself never moves with territory — only the usage-rights portion does, which is why the total quote grows by a smaller percentage than the rights line does (6.48% local→national, 15.56% local→worldwide, once the flat $1,200 creative fee is folded back in).

These three rows use the calculator's own defaults for every field except territory. Change the creative fee, term, channels, exclusivity, or image count and the dollar figures move, but the relationship holds: worldwide is always exactly 1.6÷1 × the local usage-rights figure, and national always exactly 1.25÷1 × it, for any shoot priced with the same channels, term, and exclusivity.

Open the calculator and enter your own creative fee, term, channels, and exclusivity to see your own territory comparison. Nothing you enter is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or copyright advice. It does not set your rates or replace a licensing contract.

Common questions

How much more does a national license cost than a local one?

25% more, because the territory multiplier goes from 1× for local to 1.25× for national and nothing else in the formula changes. On a $1,200 creative fee, 6-month web-only, non-exclusive license with 5 final images, local territory prices the usage rights at $420.00 ($1,620.00 total, $84.00 per image); national prices the same shoot at $525.00 in rights ($1,725.00 total, $105.00 per image).

How much more does a worldwide license cost than a local one?

60% more, from the worldwide territory multiplier of 1.6× against local's 1×. On the same $1,200/6-month/web-only/non-exclusive/5-image shoot, worldwide territory prices usage rights at $672.00 ($1,872.00 total, $134.40 per image) versus $420.00 in rights ($1,620.00 total, $84.00 per image) for local.

For independent photographers

Price the rights, not just the shoot.

When a client asks where, how long, and how widely they can use your images, turn that scope into a transparent starting quote instead of guessing.

After using this, you can now explain a commercial image license line by line, which used to take rebuilding a spreadsheet for every client request.

01

Scope the job

Where will the images appear?
02

Review the starting point

Suggested total quote
Creative / production
Usage rights
Per-image rights allocation

Client-ready draft

This is a negotiation starting point, not a contract. Define deliverables, permitted uses, credit, renewal, payment, and termination in your signed agreement.

Common questions

Start with the business value and scope of the license, not only the hours spent shooting. A paid advertising campaign, national territory, long term, or exclusivity gives the client more commercial reach and restricts how you can reuse the work. This worksheet makes those assumptions visible so you can adjust them to your market and relationship.

How is the usage-rights fee calculated?

Usage rights are 35% of the creative fee, scaled by four multipliers: the average factor of the channels you selected, the square root of the license term in months divided by six, the territory multiplier, and the exclusivity multiplier, then increased by the rush percentage. The creative/production fee itself is not scaled — only the usage-rights portion moves with scope. On a $1,200 creative fee with a 6-month national web license and non-exclusive rights, that is $525 in rights and a $1,725 total.

Why does checking more channels not just add their prices together?

The channel factor blends the highest-priced selected channel with a smaller share of the rest — 0.85× the highest factor plus 0.15× the sum of every selected channel's factor — rather than a plain average or a sum. That keeps a single channel priced exactly as it always was: checking web only (factor 1) still prices at factor 1. It also guarantees adding any channel can only raise the price, never lower it, whichever channel you already had selected — a plain average failed this, because an outdoor-only licence (factor 1.6) got cheaper once web was added, since 1.6 and 1 average to 1.3. On the $1,200/6-month/national/non-exclusive example, adding paid, print, and outdoor to web moves the factor from 1 to 2.1475, for $1,127.44 in rights and a $2,327.44 total — well short of four separate licenses, but never less than pricing the priciest channel on its own.

Why doesn't doubling the license term double the price?

Term uses a square-root scale — the multiplier is the square root of (months ÷ 6) — so it grows slower than the term itself. A 1-month license prices at about 0.41× the 6-month baseline, not 1/6th, and a 24-month license prices at 2× the baseline, not 4×. On the default $1,200/national/web/non-exclusive example, with only the term changed, rights are $214.33 at 1 month, $525 at 6 months, $742.46 at 12 months, and $1,050 at 24 months.

What is the difference between category-exclusive and fully exclusive?

Category-exclusive (1.35×) means no other business in the client's specific category can license these images for the selected channels and term — a competing brand in the same category is locked out, but an unrelated business is not. Fully exclusive (1.75×) locks out everyone, including the photographer's own future resale or stock licensing of the same images for that scope. Non-exclusive (1×) means you can license the same images to other clients. This tool applies the multiplier; the actual exclusivity terms belong in the signed contract.

Does the rush premium apply to the whole quote or just the usage-rights portion?

Only the usage-rights portion. The creative/production fee is unaffected by the rush percentage; it is the licensing calculation — channel, term, territory, and exclusivity — that gets multiplied by (1 + rush% ÷ 100). A 50% rush premium on the $1,200/national/web/6-month/non-exclusive baseline raises rights from $525 to $787.50, and the total from $1,725 to $1,987.50.

Does this replace a licensing contract?

No. It produces a quote draft and records your assumptions so you and the client start the conversation from the same numbers. You remain responsible for the signed agreement — defining the specific images, permitted uses, credit, renewal, payment terms, model releases, and termination. Ask a qualified lawyer about contract and copyright questions specific to your situation.

Where is my quote and draft stored?

In this browser's local storage only, when you click Save draft locally. Nothing is uploaded to a server — there is no account and no backend. Closing the tab does not lose a saved draft; it reloads the next time you open this page in the same browser. Clearing your browser's site data removes it. “Copy share link” is a separate option for handing the scope to someone else: it encodes the same fields into this page's own URL, so opening the link reopens the form with those fields filled in — still nothing sent to any server.

Can I use this for stock or per-image licensing instead of a project quote?

It is built for a commissioned project: one creative fee plus a usage-rights calculation, with a per-image figure shown only as an allocation of that total. Stock and microstock licensing is usually priced per download against a published rate card rather than derived from a shoot's creative fee, so this worksheet is a starting point to adapt, not a stock pricing tool.

See the territory multiplier worked into a full table: how much more does a national or worldwide license cost than local?

Already have fotoQuote Pro, or wondering whether to buy it? See this calculator vs. fotoQuote Pro.

Just tack on a flat percentage for usage? See this calculator vs. a flat usage fee.

Privacy and usage

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers and draft are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. “Copy share link” encodes your inputs into this page's own URL fragment rather than sending them anywhere — the fragment is never included in any network request, so nothing leaves your browser when you share it. We count only anonymous feature events in local storage, never people or quote content. The counter is off-switchable:

Pricing a one-off event booking instead of a licensing scope? The photo booth event quote calculator prices setup and teardown time, travel, attendant labor, and the print cost an unlimited-print package depends on — nothing uploaded. vs-a-flat-usage-fee.html.text:
← Commercial Photography Licensing Quote Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat usage fee

"Just add 25% for usage" is not a price for a license — it is a price for one narrow scope, quietly applied to a worldwide, fully exclusive, multi-channel license.

What a flat usage-fee percentage is

A flat usage add-on — 20%, 25%, sometimes "double the day rate" — is the fastest way to quote a client without opening a spreadsheet: one round number, tacked onto the creative fee, easy to say out loud on a call.

The number behind it was set with one scope in mind — usually a short term, one city, a single low-value channel, and no exclusivity — and then reused for every license afterward, whether or not the next client wants a year of paid advertising across the whole country or a two-year worldwide exclusive.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter your creative or production fee, the channels the client can use the images in, the license term, territory, exclusivity, and any rush need, and it prices usage rights separately from the creative fee — scaling with each of those — and returns a total and a per-image price for this license, not a generic one.

LicenseFlat 25% add-onWalk-away totalVerdict
$1,200 creative fee, 1 month, local, non-exclusive, web only, no rush$1,500.00$1,371.46Covers, $128.54 to spare
$1,200 creative fee, 6 months, national, non-exclusive, web only (this calculator's own default job)$1,500.00$1,725.00Short $225.00
$1,200 creative fee, 24 months, worldwide, fully exclusive, all four channels, 20% rush$1,500.00$7,261.10Short $5,761.10

Worked using this calculator's own arithmetic at a fixed $1,200 creative fee — the form's own shipped default, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the middle row: it is this calculator's own shipped starting point, not a scope picked to prove a point, and a flat 25% add-on already falls short of it. One more channel, a longer term, or exclusivity is the difference between a flat percentage that happens to work and one that does not.

What a flat usage-fee percentage doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same percentage whether the client wants web-only for a month or broadcast, print, and paid advertising for two years. Blends the channels selected into a factor that can only rise as more channels are added, and never prices a broader license as cheaper than a narrower one.
Has no separate line for license term, so a one-month license and a two-year license quote the same. Scales usage rights by the square root of the term in months over six, so a longer term costs more without punishing a short one.
Prices "a license" the same whether it covers one city or the whole world. Applies a territory multiplier — local, national, or worldwide — on top of the channel and term factors.
Has no line for exclusivity, so locking out every other business costs the same as licensing the same images to other clients too. Applies a separate exclusivity multiplier for non-exclusive, category-exclusive, or fully exclusive terms.
Gives the client a number to negotiate against, not a breakdown to defend when the scope turns out to be a two-year worldwide exclusive after the flat rate was already quoted. Reports the usage-rights line and total for the license as entered, so a round percentage can be checked against the real scope before it is sent.

A flat usage-fee percentage is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a channel mix, term, territory, or exclusivity it was not set on, and "usage rights" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat percentage skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat usage-fee percentage get the price wrong?

Because usage-rights value scales with the channels a client can use the images in, the license term, the territory, exclusivity, and any rush need — not with the creative fee alone. A one-month, local, non-exclusive, single-channel license is a different scope from a two-year, worldwide, fully exclusive license across four channels, even when the creative fee on the shoot is identical. A flat percentage prices both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat usage-fee percentage usually leave out entirely?

Which channels the client can use the images in (web is worth less than paid advertising or outdoor/broadcast), how long the license runs, whether it covers one city or the whole world, whether it locks out competitors or everyone else entirely, and any rush turnaround. A round flat percentage — 20%, 25%, "double the day rate" — is set with one scope in mind, usually a narrow one, and has no separate line for any of those.

How much do channels, term, territory, and exclusivity actually add over a flat rate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $1,200 creative fee: a narrow one-month, local, non-exclusive, web-only license walks away at $1,371.46, comfortably under a flat 25% usage add-on ($1,500.00). This calculator's own shipped default job — the same $1,200 creative fee, a 6-month national web license, non-exclusive — walks away at $1,725.00, $225.00 over that same flat 25% number. A 24-month worldwide, fully exclusive license across all four channels with a 20% rush walks away at $7,261.10, $5,761.10 over a flat 25% add-on on the same $1,200 creative fee.

Is a flat usage-fee percentage ever the right way to quote?

For something close to the narrow scope it was probably set on — a short term, one city, non-exclusive, a single low-value channel — a flat percentage can land close or leave room to spare, and on this calculator's own numbers that easy license clears a flat 25% add-on with over a hundred dollars to spare. The risk is a longer term, a wider territory, exclusivity, or extra channels stacking on top of each other, because a flat percentage has no way to see any of them until the client has already been quoted.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on going rates for photography or licensing in any market. It takes the creative fee, channels, term, territory, exclusivity, and rush need you enter and turns them into a usage-rights breakdown and total for the license you describe — the arithmetic a flat percentage skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat usage-fee percentage is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the scope stops matching the license it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

vs-fotoquote.html.text:
← Commercial Photography Licensing Quote Calculator

This calculator vs. fotoQuote Pro

Two different starting points: fotoQuote Pro tells you what a licence is worth from a market-rate database. This page turns a creative fee you already have into a transparent usage-rights breakdown for one client.

What each tool is for

fotoQuote Pro, from Cradoc fotoSoftware, is a long-established pricing-guide application photographers buy once and install on Windows or Mac (a separate subscription version, fotoQuote 8i, runs on iOS). It ships with a market-rate database spanning hundreds of stock-licensing categories and assignment types, and its job is answering what should I charge from that data, described on the publisher's own product page. It is a one-time purchase with a money-back guarantee rather than a subscription, and free demos are available before buying.

This calculator does not have a pricing database and does not tell you what your work is worth — that is not the job it does. It starts from a creative or production fee you already have in mind for a commissioned project, then turns the client's requested usage — which channels, how long, how wide a territory, and whether the licence is exclusive — into a transparent usage-rights line and a client-ready draft. It runs free in any browser, needs no purchase and no install, and nothing you type leaves your device.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is a fair market rate for this stock photo, or this assignment type, before I have quoted anything?fotoQuote Pro — its job is a market-rate pricing database this calculator does not have.
I already have a creative fee in mind for this shoot — what should the usage-rights portion be for the channels, term, territory and exclusivity this client wants?This calculator — enter the fee and the scope, get the breakdown and a client-ready draft, free, with no install.
How much more does national or worldwide usage cost than local, on the same shoot?This calculator's territory worked table.
What is stock or microstock licensing worth per download against a published rate card?fotoQuote Pro — this calculator is built for a commissioned project's usage rights, not per-download stock pricing.
Do I need to install anything or create an account to use the tool?This calculator: no. fotoQuote Pro is a desktop purchase and install (or an iOS subscription for the mobile reference version).

Most photographers get more use out of both, for different jobs: a market-rate guide like fotoQuote for deciding what a shoot or a stock image is worth in the first place, and a scope worksheet like this one for showing a specific client, line by line, why their requested usage costs what it costs once a creative fee is already agreed.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or fotoQuote Pro?

They start from different places. fotoQuote Pro, from Cradoc fotoSoftware, is a paid desktop app you buy once and install on Windows or Mac; its job is telling you what a licence is worth from a market-rate database covering hundreds of stock categories and assignment types, described on the publisher's own site. This calculator does not have a pricing database and does not tell you what your work is worth. It starts from a creative or production fee you already have in mind, then turns the client's channels, term, territory, exclusivity, and rush need into a transparent usage-rights breakdown and a client-ready draft, free, in your browser, with nothing to install. A photographer figuring out what to charge from scratch is better served by a market-rate guide like fotoQuote; a photographer who already has a day rate or project fee and needs to show a specific client how the requested usage scope changes the price is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with fotoQuote or Cradoc fotoSoftware?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Cradoc fotoSoftware. fotoQuote is a registered trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
